title: Concept Drills — Biomolecules & Cell Biology (Class 11 Biology)
subject: biology

questions.concept: Why the cell membrane is a fluid mosaic
questions.question: Why is the membrane described as 'fluid' and 'mosaic' — what do the two words each refer to?
questions.solution: FLUID: phospholipids and proteins move laterally within the bilayer — the membrane is a 2D liquid, not a rigid wall (fluidity tuned by cholesterol and unsaturated tails). MOSAIC: a patchwork of proteins (integral, peripheral) embedded at different depths, each with its own job. The model replaces the old rigid 'sandwich' idea.

questions.question: Why does the mitochondrion have TWO membranes with different properties, and what does the inner membrane's folding achieve?
questions.solution: The outer membrane is a permeable boundary; the inner membrane is the working surface — it holds the electron-transport chain and is impermeable to ions, allowing a proton gradient to build. Cristae (folds) multiply that surface area, packing more ATP-producing machinery per organelle. Compartmentalisation + surface area = efficient chemiosmosis.

questions.question: Root cells accumulate mineral ions at concentrations far higher than the soil. Which transport mechanism achieves this and what does it require?
questions.solution: ACTIVE transport — carrier proteins move ions AGAINST the concentration gradient, which is thermodynamically uphill and therefore requires ATP. Passive diffusion can only equalise concentrations, never exceed them. Accumulation against a gradient is the defining signature of active uptake.

questions.concept: Enzyme specificity and the active site
questions.question: Why does an enzyme catalyse one reaction but not a closely related one?
questions.solution: The active site's shape and chemical groups complement ONE substrate (lock-and-key/induced fit): binding positions the substrate's bonds next to catalytic groups and stabilises the transition state, lowering Ea. A non-fitting substrate is neither positioned nor activated. Shape complementarity + transition-state stabilisation = specificity.

questions.question: Name the four levels of protein structure and the bond/interaction responsible for each.
questions.solution: Primary: amino-acid sequence (peptide bonds). Secondary: α-helix/β-sheet (H-bonds in the backbone). Tertiary: overall 3D fold (hydrophobic clustering, disulphide bridges, ionic and H-bonds between side chains). Quaternary: multiple subunits assembled (same non-covalent forces between chains, e.g. haemoglobin's four).

questions.question: Why do cells not grow indefinitely large, even when nutrients are plentiful?
questions.solution: Volume grows as the cube of linear dimension while surface area grows only as the square, so the surface-to-volume ratio falls as a cell enlarges. Exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes across the membrane then cannot keep pace with the volume's demand. Small size preserves a workable surface-to-volume ratio — geometry, not materials, sets the ceiling.

questions.question: Diffusion moves substances down a gradient for free — why must active transport be paid for?
questions.solution: Moving a solute against its concentration gradient decreases entropy locally, which cannot happen spontaneously; the cell must spend free energy to drive it. ATP hydrolysis couples to pump proteins, changing their conformation so the solute is forced uphill. Diffusion is downhill and free; active transport is uphill and must be bought with ATP.

questions.question: An enzyme catalyses thousands of reactions yet is recovered unchanged. What does that imply about how it works?
questions.solution: The enzyme only lowers the activation energy by providing a favourable transition-state environment; it is not a reactant, so it emerges as it entered. That is exactly why a tiny amount suffices and why catalysts are called reusable. Enzymes change the PATH, not the participants.
